0: After you get the first result running, it is tempting to try a bigger model. But switching from 0.5B to 7B may no longer fit the machine you have.
1: When choosing resources, separate a few things first. The CPU and GPU do the computing, memory and VRAM hold the data in use, and the disk stores the model files. Being able to download a model only means the disk has room; whether it runs smoothly depends on memory, VRAM and compute. For the same model, the load precision, the input length and how many requests run at once all affect resource use. Inference and training also have different needs.
2: Below we look at what CPU and GPU are each good at, then work out how much space a model's parameters take, as preparation for choosing a laptop or a cloud instance later.
5: CPU and GPU differ noticeably in how they compute.
6: The CPU targets general computing: each core has fairly complete control and arithmetic capability, can branch, jump and schedule work according to the program's execution, and can handle different kinds of computation flexibly.
7: The GPU uses a parallel architecture with a very large number of compute units that can run many computations at once. It suits tasks with large data volumes and highly repetitive computation.
9: How fast a CPU or GPU is depends on the task type and the scale of computation.
10: For scenarios with lots of logical decisions, program control and task scheduling, the CPU is more efficient. Tasks such as running an operating system or querying a database are well suited to the CPU.
11: For large-scale parallel computation the GPU provides higher throughput. Matrix multiplication and convolution in deep learning can be split into many parallel sub-tasks executed at once by GPU compute units, raising overall efficiency.
12: Still, the GPU's advantage only becomes clear when the computation is large enough. With small data volumes the GPU's compute resources cannot be fully used, and data transfer between CPU and GPU plus task scheduling add overhead, so the CPU may be more efficient.
14: The cost of CPU and GPU is not only the purchase price of the hardware, but also the power consumed while running and the later use and maintenance cost.
15: On hardware purchase, the CPU is standard equipment: ordinary servers and personal computers both need one. High-performance GPUs for AI training and inference are usually expensive, and besides the GPU itself you have to count the cost of servers, VRAM, storage and other supporting hardware.
16: While running, a GPU doing large-scale computation draws a lot of power; the more GPUs in a server, the greater the pressure on power and cooling, and the electricity and cooling cost of a data centre rises markedly.
17: On use and maintenance, the CPU ecosystem is mature and routine server maintenance is fairly simple. GPUs require compatibility between drivers, compute frameworks and the hardware environment, and conflicts between versions can stop a model running normally. Multi-GPU environments also involve data communication between devices, which makes demands on hardware connections and software configuration.
19: Training and inference have different resource requirements, and models of different sizes and types differ greatly too. Hardware selection has to weigh model size, data volume, performance requirements and the needs of both training and inference.
20: In the training stage, with small data volumes a CPU can meet the training needs of most traditional machine-learning models, such as linear regression, logistic regression and random forests. Some lightweight neural networks can also be trained on a CPU, but as data volume and model complexity grow, training time lengthens noticeably. If you need to tune models frequently, a GPU shortens training time.
21: Training large neural networks and large language models involves a great deal of matrix computation and demands high compute and VRAM. A model with billions of parameters such as Qwen needs high-performance accelerators like GPUs to train.
22: At inference the hardware requirements differ from training. For scenarios with a smaller model and low traffic, a CPU is enough for inference, and methods such as quantization can lower resource use further. For large models, high-concurrency services and scenarios needing fast responses, a GPU gives higher inference efficiency.
23: CPU and GPU each have their scenarios; weigh model size, data volume, concurrent requests, performance requirements and deployment cost together.
26: Assessing a model's resource needs comes down mainly to two things: parameter scale and data precision.
27: Parameter scale is usually written with B, where 1B means one billion parameters. Parameters are the numbers the model learned during training; at inference they must be loaded into memory (CPU) or VRAM (GPU). The more parameters, the more resources are used.
28: Data precision refers to the numeric format used to store and compute the model's parameters. Common formats include FP32, FP16 and BF16, and INT8 and INT4 for quantization. For the same parameter count, higher precision uses more resources.

46: Model weights = parameter count × the storage per 1B parameters at that precision. Taking a 7B model at FP16 for inference, the weights take about: 7 × 2GB ≈ 14GB.
47: Besides loading the model weights, inference also needs extra resources for the KV cache, the runtime framework and temporary computation.
48: The KV cache stores information about tokens already computed during generation, avoiding recomputation. Its size relates to the model structure, the context length and the number of concurrent requests. The longer the context, the more information must be kept; the more requests handled at once, the more the KV cache grows.
49: The formula for estimating inference resource use:
50: Memory needed for CPU inference ≈ model weights + framework and temporary overhead.
51: VRAM needed for GPU inference ≈ model weights + KV cache + framework and temporary overhead.
52: The weights are static and framework overhead is basically constant, so the variable is all in the KV cache. In long-sequence scenarios, space must be reserved for the KV cache.
54: The training stage needs more resources than inference. Besides storing the model weights, it must store gradients, optimizer state and intermediate results, so it needs more. The requirement depends on the optimizer type and the training strategy.

68: Note: the Adam optimizer stores two FP32 states (momentum and variance), so optimizer state takes 8GB; the FP32 weight copy is used for the optimizer's parameter update.
69: The rough formula for full training is:
70: VRAM needed for GPU training ≈ parameter count × 16 Byte + activation overhead
71: Memory needed for CPU training ≈ parameter count × 16 Byte + activation overhead
72: GPU training is limited by VRAM capacity, while CPU training is limited by compute speed. For example, full FP16 training of a 7B model on a GPU needs at least 7B × 16 Byte ≈ 112GB of VRAM, and with activations the real requirement is larger.
74: For large-model fine-tuning, parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) are more common in practice. LoRA does not update all the original model's parameters; it freezes the original weights and trains only the added low-rank adaptation parameters, so the VRAM requirement drops markedly.
75: LoRA training VRAM ≈ base model weights + LoRA parameters + LoRA parameter gradients and optimizer state + activations.
76: Here the base model weights only need loading and are not updated; LoRA adds only 0.1%-1% of the original parameters, so its gradient and optimizer overhead is almost negligible. Actual VRAM mainly depends on the model weights, the context length, the batch size and the framework's optimisation, and LoRA fine-tuning lowers the VRAM requirement markedly compared with full training.
77: For example, loading a 7B model at FP16 takes about 4GB of weights. On a single GPU with 24GB of VRAM, LoRA fine-tuning can usually run (with the batch size and context length adjusted). Using QLoRA (quantizing the base model to INT4) lowers the footprint further, so fine-tuning fits even more limited hardware.
